title: Illuminating the Effects of Dynamic Lighting on Student Learning
research_question: To evaluate the effect of a dynamic artificial lighting system's 'focus' setting on student concentration, motivation, and oral reading fluency (ORF) performance in classrooms.

participants.description: 84 third graders, ages 7 to 8, from a public school in the midsouth region of the United States.
participants.recruitment: Four classrooms were randomly assigned, two to each condition (focus or normal lighting).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Classrooms equipped with dynamic lighting systems. 'Focus' lighting: 1000 lux, 6500K CCT (Modified Softrace with three T5HO lamps). 'Normal' lighting: 500 lux, 3500K CCT (lens troffer 2 by 4 two-lamp T8 fluorescent fixtures). Other settings (calm, energy) were available but focus was primary for treatment.

measures.instrument: AIMSweb Curriculum-Based Measurement (CBM) Test of ORF (words read correctly per minute)
Motivation Questionnaire (adapted from Pintrich and DeGroot, 1990)

findings.antecedent: Focus lighting (1000 lux, 6500K CCT) during instruction vs. Normal lighting (500 lux, 3500K CCT) during instruction
findings.consequent: Oral Reading Fluency (ORF) performance (words read correctly per minute)
findings.mechanism: Focus light setting as an instructional technology improved the reading performance of the experimental group at a rate greater than the control group.

findings.antecedent: Focus lighting (1000 lux, 6500K CCT) during instruction vs. Normal lighting (500 lux, 3500K CCT) during instruction
findings.quote: For concentration and motivation, we found no lighting by testing occasion interaction effects.

findings.antecedent: Focus lighting (1000 lux, 6500K CCT) during instruction vs. Normal lighting (500 lux, 3500K CCT) during instruction
findings.quote: Repeated measures ANOVA test for the effect of concentration was not significant, F(2, 1.84) = 225.4, mean standard error = 1203.5, p = .08.

mechanisms: Improved reading performance due to focus light setting as an instructional technology, possibly by enhancing concentration/focus.
moderators: Testing occasion (longitudinal effect over the school year)
implementation_implications: Light qualities of illumination and color temperature influence student gains in reading.
Educational and industrial designers should consider how to select lighting for optimizing teaching and learning.
Further evaluation of illumination level and color temperature variables on student learning outcomes is needed.

tables.description: ORF results showing WCPM over three testing occasions for Focus and Normal lighting groups.

limitations: Quasi-experimental design, unable to control for teacher effects.
All students were tested in a normal lighting environment, potentially disadvantaging the focus lighting group due to encoding specificity.
Only one measure used for each dependent variable, potentially leading to poor measures for motivation and concentration.
Students and teachers may have been aware of the study, potentially conforming to desired outcomes (threat to internal validity).
d2 Test of Concentration may not be valid for students under age 9 (average age in study was closer to 8).

paper_metadata.title: Illuminating the Effects of Dynamic Lighting on Student Learning
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Illuminating the Effects of Dynamic Lighting on Student Learning
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Light is universally understood as essential to the human condition. Yet light quality varies substantially in nature and in controlled environments leading to questions of which artificial light characteristics facilitate maximum learning. Recent research has examined lighting variables of color temperature, and illumination for affecting sleep, mood, focus, motivation, concentration, and work and school performance. This has resulted in artificial light systems intended to support human beings in their actualization through dynamic lighting technology allowing for different lighting conditions per task. A total of 84 third graders were exposed to either focus (6000K-100fc average maintained) or normal lighting. Focus lighting led to a higher percentage increase in oral reading fluency performance (36%) than did control lighting (17%). No lighting effects were found for motivation or concentration, possibly attributable to the younger age level of respondents as compared with European studies. These findings illuminate the need for further research on artificial light and learning.

stimulus_description.duration_exposure: continuous during school hours for one academic year
control_conditions: Standard static fluorescent classroom lighting (approx. 300-500 lux, 4000K CCT)

theory_commitments.theory_name: Non-visual effects of light on human physiology and cognition
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Specific light parameters (e.g., CCT, illuminance) influence human alertness, mood, and cognitive function through non-visual pathways, thereby affecting learning outcomes.

mechanism_chain.description: Dynamic lighting conditions influence physiological arousal and alertness, which in turn affects students' attention and on-task behavior, ultimately impacting academic performance.

steps.from_construct: Dynamic lighting conditions (e.g., higher CCT, illuminance)
steps.to_construct: Physiological arousal and alertness (e.g., melatonin suppression)
Improved attention and reduced off-task behavior
